groups.text: Netty is the select loop from the last lesson, written well.
An event loop is one thread that runs a selector over many channels, plus a queue of tasks.
Each new connection is registered with one loop for life.
So all of a channel's events run on that one thread, one after another, and handlers rarely need locks.
Every channel also has a pipeline: a list of handlers between a head, next to the socket, and a tail.
Inbound events start at the head and move toward the tail.
The first read brings three bytes.
The frame decoder keeps them, because the line has not ended.
The next read brings the end of the line and the start of another.
Now the decoder passes on one ByteBuf, hello, and keeps the rest.
The string decoder turns it into a String.
The read skips the encoder, which only handles writes.
Your handler sees whole lines.
Writes go the other way.
Your handler calls ctx.writeAndFlush, and the message moves toward the head.
The string encoder turns the String back into bytes, and the head hands them to the socket.
So reads see the handlers in the order you added them, and writes see them in reverse.
One thread runs every handler of every channel on its loop.
So never block in a handler.
Client A asks for SLOW, and the handler sleeps for one second, standing in for a JDBC call.
Client B asks for FAST, fifty milliseconds later.
The loop thread is stuck in A's handler, so it cannot even read B's request.
B's reply takes one thousand eleven milliseconds.
The fix is to hand the slow part to your own executor.
The loop thread is free at once, and FAST comes back in two milliseconds.
In code: leave the loop, block in your pool, and write the reply from there.
Netty sees the write is not on the loop thread, and queues it as a task on the channel's own loop.
